question.prompt: Forty slips are placed into a hat, each bearing a number \(1,\) \(2,\) \(3,\) \(4,\) \(5,\) \(6,\) \(7,\) \(8,\) \(9,\) or \(10,\) with each number entered on four slips. Four slips are drawn from the hat at random and without replacement. Let \(p\) be the probability that all four slips bear the same number. Let \(q\) be the probability that two of the slips bear a number \(a\) and the other two bear a number \(b \ne a.\) What is the value of \(\dfrac{q}{p}?\)

solutions.explanation:
Treat the forty physical slips as distinct, even when their printed numbers agree. Every ordered draw of four distinct slips is equally likely. Each four-slip set can be drawn in \(4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1=24\) orders, so all four-slip sets are equally likely as well.

Let \(T\) be the total number of four-slip sets. To get four equal numbers, choose the printed number in \(10\) ways, then take all four of its slips. Hence
\[
p=\frac{10}{T}>0.
\]
For two pairs, first choose the two different printed numbers as an unordered pair. There are \(10\cdot9/2=45\) choices. For each number, choose two of its four slips in \(4\cdot3/2=6\) ways. In each pair count, division by \(2\) removes the two possible orders of the same pair.

Thus there are \(45\cdot6\cdot6=1620\) favorable sets. Every two-pair set determines its two printed numbers and its two pairs of physical slips uniquely, so none is omitted or counted twice. Therefore
\[
\frac qp
=\frac{1620/T}{10/T}
=162.
\]
The answer is \(162\), choice \(\mathrm{A}\).
solutions.title: Compare counts with a common denominator
